input:
A flat stainless steel wall with a thickness of 150 mm separates two process streams from one another. The thermal conductivity of the wall material is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 324 K. Under conditions of steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through a flat wall of this kind is proportional to the thermal conductivity and to the temperature difference, and inversely proportional to the thickness of the wall. Based on the values stated above, the resulting heat flux works out to 34560 W m⁻².

It should be noted that surface (film) resistances have been excluded from this particular estimate. The figure of 34560 W m⁻² therefore represents the flux through the metal alone, corresponding to the measured temperature difference across the metal itself. If the film resistances were included, the flux would be lower, since the films add further resistance in series with the wall while the overall temperature difference between the two streams remains fixed. Overall, the estimate is most appropriate in situations where the resistance of the wall dominates the heat-flow path; where the films dominate instead, the wall-only figure will overstate the flux by the share that the films carry.
target:
A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 324 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall gives a heat flux proportional to the conductivity and to the temperature difference, and inversely proportional to the thickness. On the stated values the heat flux is 34560 W m⁻².

Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate. The flux of 34560 W m⁻² is therefore the flux through the metal alone, at the measured difference across the metal. Including the film resistances lowers the flux, because the films add resistance in series with the wall while the overall temperature difference between the streams stays fixed. The estimate serves where the wall resistance dominates the path; where the films dominate, the wall-only figure overstates the flux by the share the films carry.

The thickness enters the estimate directly: a wall twice as thick at the same conductivity and the same temperature difference passes half the flux, and the relation is used in that form when walls of different thickness are compared on the same duty. The conductivity is taken as constant across the wall, so the temperature profile through the metal is a straight line and the measured difference fixes the gradient everywhere in the metal. Where conductivity varies with temperature across the wall, the constant-value estimate is an approximation whose error follows the variation, and a mean conductivity over the span is the correction the simple form admits.
